<meta>This page contains verses 498 to 507 of the Therigatha, specifically from the verses attributed to Sumedha. The text uses metaphors to illustrate the vastness of suffering in the cycle of rebirth and the dangers of sensual pleasures.</meta>

# VERSES OF THE ELDER NUNS

Remember that in the beginningless <term>samsara</term> <gloss>cycle of birth and death</gloss>, if the earth of the Rose-apple Island <note>original: "Jambudipa", referring to the Indian subcontinent or the known world</note> were rolled into little balls the size of jujube stones, they would not be enough to represent all the mothers and fathers one has had. 498.

Remember that if all the grass, wood, branches, and leaves were gathered from the beginningless cycle and cut into finger-length pieces, they would not be enough to represent all the fathers and grandfathers one has had. 499.

Remember the blind turtle in the eastern ocean and the yoke-hole in the western ocean; the chance of the turtle putting its head through that hole is the comparison used for the rarity of obtaining a human birth. 500.

Remember that the physical form is like a lump of foam, a body of misery and without substance; look at the <term>khandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of existence</gloss> as impermanent, and remember the many afflictions in the hells. 501.

Remember those who fill up the cemeteries again and again in various births; remember the fears of the crocodiles <note>a metaphor for the dangers of the world</note>, and remember the Four Noble Truths. 502.

While the Deathless <note>Nirvana</note> exists, why do you drink the five bitter things? For all sensual delights are more bitter than those five bitter medicines. 503.

While the Deathless exists, what use to you are sensual pleasures which are burning fevers? For all sensual delights are blazing, boiling, disturbed, and inflamed. 504.

While there is a state of no enmity, what use to you are sensual pleasures which have many enemies? Sensual pleasures are shared with kings, fire, thieves, water, and unloved heirs; they have many enemies. 505.

While liberation exists, what use to you are sensual pleasures which involve execution and imprisonment? For in sensual pleasures there is execution and imprisonment; those who crave sensual pleasures experience many sufferings. 506.

A grass torch, when lit, burns the one who holds it if they do not let go; sensual pleasures are like that torch, they burn those who do not let go of them. 507.

Do not, for the sake of a small amount of sensual happiness, abandon a vast happiness.

Do not be like a broad-finned fish that swallows the hook and is later destroyed. <note>The broad-finned fish is a traditional metaphor for one who is lured by sensory pleasure only to find it leads to suffering.</note> Restrain yourself from sensual desires, or they will treat you like a dog bound by a chain. Indeed, these desires will devour you just as the <term>Candala</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss> treat a hungry dog.

You will experience immeasurable suffering and many mental distresses if you remain attached to sensual pleasures. Renounce these unstable desires. Since the ageless state exists, what use have you for these pleasures that are subject to decay? All births, in all places, are seized by death and disease.

This <note>the state of Nibbana</note> is ageless; this is undying; this is the ageless and undying state that is free from sorrow. It is without enemies, without confinement, without stumbling, without fear, and without affliction. This deathless state has been attained by many and can still be obtained today by one who applies themselves with thorough attention <note>original: <term>yoniso</term></note>. But it cannot be reached by one who does not strive.

Thus spoke Sumedha, finding no delight in conditioned things. While Anikaratta <note>the prince who wished to marry her</note> was pleading with her, Sumedha cut off her hair and threw it on the ground. <note>Cutting the hair is a symbolic act of renouncing worldly life and beauty to become a nun.</note>

Anikaratta stood up and, with hands pressed together in respect, begged her father: "Let Sumedha go, so that she may go forth into the homeless life to see the truth of liberation."

Released by her mother and father, she went forth into the homeless life, fearing sorrow and danger. While still a student, she realized the six higher powers <note>original: <term>abhiññā</term></note> and reached the highest fruit <note>Arahantship, or full enlightenment</note>.

Marvelous and wonderful was the <term>Nibbana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss> of that princess. In her final hour, she explained her conduct in previous lives:

"In the time of the Blessed One Konagamana <note>a Buddha of a previous age</note>, in a newly built monastery, three of us friends gave the gift of a dwelling place. Ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, and ten thousand times we were reborn among the gods. What need is there to mention our births among humans? Among the gods, we possessed great psychic power. What need is there to mention our status among humans?"

<summary>The nun Sumedha rejects a royal marriage, cuts her hair in renunciation, and achieves enlightenment. She recounts her past merit of donating a monastery during the time of a previous Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Sumedha, Therigatha, renunciation, Nibbana, Konagamana Buddha, merit, rebirth</keywords>

I was the woman-treasure, the chief queen of the Lord of the Seven Treasures <note>original: "Sattaratanassa mahesī itthiratanam ahaṃ āsi." This refers to the consort of a Universal Monarch or Cakkavatti.</note>. 520.
That was the cause, that was the source, that was the root: patience in the teaching of the Teacher. That was the first meeting; that was the Nirvana for one delighted in the Dhamma. 521.
Thus they speak, those who have faith in the word of the One of Supreme Wisdom. They grow weary of existence; having grown weary, they become dispassionate. 522.

She spoke these verses. There, in the city of Mantāvatī <note>original: "Mantāvatiyā nagare"</note> means in the city named Mantāvatī. Of King Koñca <note>original: "Rañño Koñcassa"</note> means she was the daughter born from the womb of the chief queen of the king named Koñca. By name, she was Sumedhā. Pleasing through the practitioners of the teaching <note>original: "Pāsādikā sāsanakārehī"</note> means she was one who had gained confidence in the Triple Gem through the noble ones who practice the Teacher's instruction and through the preaching of the Dhamma.

Virtuous <note>original: "Silavatī"</note> means endowed with conduct and morality. Eloquent <note>original: "Cittakathā"</note> means her talk on the Dhamma was variegated and beautiful. Learned <note>original: "Bahussutā"</note> means she was well-established in the scriptures. Disciplined in the Buddha's teaching <note>original: "Buddhasāsane vinītā"</note> means she was disciplined in the teaching of the Buddhas because her defilements were removed through wise attention following the discourses, understanding how one goes forth, how one attains Nirvana, and what constitutes morality, concentration, and wisdom. Her body, speech, and mind were restrained. Listen, both of you <note>original: "Ubhayo nisāmethā"</note> means you two should listen to my words. The construction is: she spoke having approached her mother and father.

Even if it is divine <note>original: "Yadi pi dibbaṃ"</note> means even that which belongs to the heavenly worlds, everything included in existence, is impermanent, unstable, suffering, and subject to change. How much more so the empty sensual pleasures? <note>original: "Kim aṅgaṃ pana tucchā kāmā"</note> means how much more so are human pleasures? Because they are essentially unpleasant, they are empty and hollow. They are like a drop of honey on the edge of a sword, providing little taste but resulting in great suffering and much distress now and in the future.

Bitter <note>original: "Kaṭukā"</note> means undesirable; they are like venomous snakes because of their fearful nature. Infatuated with which pleasures <note>original: "Yesu kāmesu mucchitā"</note> means those who are stuck in them. It is ingrained in human nature to desire many things, a desire that cannot be satisfied except through the knowledge of new things and, as follows from this, through admiration and inquiry. Thus, we neglect what is common and obvious, while new and distant things please us. In order for men not alien to letters to satisfy this, without turning the love of learning into idle curiosity—which sometimes examines things whose knowledge is of little use—they adopted this caution: to mix the useful with the sweet and the sweet with the useful, and to select the subjects of their Academic discourses, singular in both their utility and their rarity. In this part, they imitate the Emperor in § 3 of the Preface to the Institutes, who thought the minds of students should be led from ancient fables to more weighty and useful matters. Following them, I have decided for this time to offer a certain tasting of the theme of **ALTERO TANTO** <gloss>the other as much/double</gloss>, which commends itself sufficiently by its rarity and utility, and to reserve a fuller treatment of the same for another time. May it be so with the help of God.

In *Law 5, § fin., ff. de Publican.*, it is *Duplum* <gloss>double</gloss>. Sometimes it is called *Bis tantum* <gloss>twice as much</gloss>, *tantundem amplius* <gloss>as much again more</gloss>, etc. (Calvin, in *Lexicon Juridicum*, under these terms, among which the more customary are *Alterum tantum* and *Duplum*).

3. Various meanings of this are found in our law: 1. It is taken broadly for any thing’s "other as much" or "other as many." In the aforementioned *Law 13, ff. de liber. et posth.*, where the inheritance is divided into seven parts according to the will, Julian says the son of the testator will have "as much again" more than the wife; likewise, the wife "as much again" more than the daughter. And thus the son received four parts, the wife two, the daughter one. That is, the son to the mother, and the mother to the daughter, were in double proportion, as Gothofredus notes on that very *Law 13*, which is called here "the other as much," and here it concerns the division of an inheritance. 2. Strictly for that double amount which is exacted in the name of a penalty, interest, or some accession. 3. Most strictly, with respect to only that accession which, in a loan, has proceeded up to the sum of the principal, which is what we shall mainly address in our inquiry.

4. With this meaning, I define "the other as much" as nothing other than such an accession, or as much of an accession, added to the principal given in a loan, as the principal sum itself is.

5. Since it is so arranged in a loan that usury agrees with the principal in regard to its matter (Hotoman, *de usur.* c. 2), and an accession of a different kind than the principal is not, strictly speaking, usury, but something given or promised in place of usury (*Law 14, 17, C. de usur.*), I have therefore said that the "other as much" agrees with the principal in quality.

6. Thus, the words themselves suggest that it is reciprocal with the principal in regard to quantity. For as soon as something is given for the sake of an accession beyond "as much again," it is no longer the "other as much," but begins to be the "third as much," if I may speak in this way. Just as it cannot be called "as much" below the equalization of the simple or principal amount, since it has not yet reached that quantity, nor is it "as much" as the principal itself is.

7. As for the opinion of Bartolus, Baldus, Castrensis, and others, who believe that *when it is said in law that usury should not exceed the double, it is understood as usury of one year*, it is easy to conjecture that nothing is more absurd, as *Fachin. 10, controversy 65* relates. For it cannot happen in such a short space of time, unless by a cruel creditor, that as much is exacted in the name of usury (for example, in a single year) as the principal debt is worth. Nor is the "other as much" or "double" considered if it consists of a smaller or not equal quantity to the principal, as has been said before.

8. Hence the controversy is declared, which holds almost the first place in this matter: Does the "simple" exist within the "other as much"? And although *Budaeus on Law 10, Code de usuris*, wished that the "simple" does not exist in this double of usury, and thus usury could run up to the double of the principal, the principal not being computed—*Molinaeus, treatise on usury, number 47*.

Having therefore implored divine aid and the assistance of the Holy Spirit before all else in this labor, I shall begin my dissertation on the nominal definition of the White Fluor, since the term Fluor in the medical forum is quite Homonymous, by starting with its homonymy. The sons of the Gods use the word Fluor broadly for every flux or falling away of peccant matter, from any part and to any part. Strictly and specifically, however, it also denotes Catarrh, or the preternatural flowing down of vicious matter collected in the head into the underlying parts. Sometimes it is taken for a species of Diarrhea and Dysentery, namely when the excrements emulate the water in which meat has been washed, and it is then called a Hepatic Flux. ## II.

Regarding synonymy, our condition acquires various other names. Hippocrates and Galen—the former indeed in *On the Nature of Woman*, Section XV, text II, and Section XLV, text I; the latter in Book III of *On the Causes of Symptoms*, and also in *On the Difference of Symptoms* and VI *On Affected Parts*—call it *rhoon* or *rhoun gynaikeion*, a flux or female fluor, perhaps because it is proper to women. In Forestus, *Observations*, Book XVIII, Observation XIX, it is called a Female Profluvium, White Superfluity, White Flowers, Female Purgation, and so forth, the reason for which denomination is clear from the words themselves. Riverius, in *Medical Practice*, Book XV, chapter IV, chose to name it a Profluvium of the Uterus. The most sagacious investigator of Nature, Gualtherus Charleton, preferred to call it Rheumatism of the Uterus. In Sylvius, *Medical Practice*, Book III, chapter IV, because of the similarity it seems to have at first glance with phlegm, it is called Phlegmatic Humor. It is also given the title by some of White Menses; but since this fluor is accustomed to be amiss more frequently outside the flux of the months, before or after the Natural Lunar Tribute has been paid, than during the menstrual time itself, with the most accurate Sylvius, we do not see why it deserves this name, except most improperly. To the Germans, it is usually called *der weisse Fluß*, and so forth; and who could recount all the names devised by so many physicians and imposed upon this condition?

The specific difference, however, is taken from the uterus, so that it may be distinguished from other rheumatic conditions, for example, coryza, broncho, catarrh, rheumatism *kat' exochen* (by eminence) so called, etc. It is evident that in this way this condition can be referred to symptoms of impaired action, to symptoms of excreta part in quantity and quality, and to symptoms of altered quality, by reason of the lividity of the face, the cadaverous appearance, etc.

->V.<-

That the subject more generally consists only of women, provided that in a broader sense virgins are also included, no one will easily call into doubt, since the male sex is accustomed to be immune from this foul disease. What part specifically is to be considered as affected, it is now my intention to inquire. The description points to the uterus, because from the uterus alone the said humors flow—now more sparse, now more copious, now bland, now acrid, now whitening, now yellowing—never by another way. Since, therefore, the uterus exists as the cause not only of this, but of all diseases (that is to say, female ones) according to the divine Coan <note>referring to Hippocrates</note>, and when the uterus is affected, the whole body is drawn into its *koinonia* (communion) and contagion, I think I shall not stray from the goal if, before I proceed to the rest, I have inquired with the strength of my small talent, briefly and in three words, into its position, magnitude, figure, substance, and connection; and a little more accurately, though still briefly, into the vessels, so that I may more happily attain the proposed end.

->VI.<-

The Position of the uterus immediately reveals a singular divine providence, while we see it placed in the hypogastrium, or the lowest part of the abdomen, between the bladder and the rectum, which are for it like two cushions, lest the tender embryo be injured by the hardness of the bones. Furthermore, that place is also most suitable not only for the growth of the conceived fetus—since when the uterus is distended into a huge mass in the final months, more space was required—but also for its exclusion once perfected.

The biography of Yizong <note>original: 義宗</note>, named Bei, states he was the eldest son of Taizu. When the Huhar kingdom surrendered, Taizu renamed the nation East Dan and appointed Bei as the Human Sovereign King to govern it. When Taizhou ascended the throne, he designated Dongping as the Southern Capital and relocated Bei to reside there. Upon Bei's return to his domain, he ordered Wang Jiyuan to compose the Southern Capital Stele.

He composed the *Garden Poetry on Making Music* and the *Langyuan Collection*.

The *History of Liao* in the Biographies of the Imperial Clan concerning King Ping, Longxian, records that King Ping was intelligent and possessed vast learning. He was capable in poetry and his writings circulated widely in the world. 

He shot ten deer and captured nine of them.

The *History of Liao* in the Biographies of the Imperial Clan concerning Qian, named Jun, states he was the eldest son of Daozong. At age six, he was enfeoffed as the King of Liang. The following year, he accompanied the Emperor on a hunt. His arrows hit the target three times in succession. The Emperor looked to his attendants and said, "Since the time of my ancestors, our riding and archery have surpassed others. Though this child is young, he does not let that tradition fall." Later, encountering the Emperor's joy, a banquet was prepared.

Cutting a Paulownia leaf to make a jade scepter.

Liu Xiang's *Garden of Stories* <note>original: Shuo Yuan</note> records that King Cheng and Tang Shuyu were living in leisure. The King cut a leaf from a paulownia tree into the shape of a jade scepter and gave it to Tang Shuyu, saying, "I use this to enfeoff you." Tang Shuyu was delighted and informed the Duke of Zhou. The Duke of Zhou requested an audience and asked, "Did the Son of Heaven enfeoff Shuyu?" King Cheng replied, "I was only joking with Shuyu." The Duke of Zhou responded, "The Son of Heaven has no joking words." Consequently, Tang Shuyu was enfeoffed at Jin.

The Great Treasure and the Secret Books.

Ying Shao's *Comprehensive Meaning of Customs* <note>original: Fengsu Tong</note> records that An, the King of Huainan, recruited thousands of guests, practitioners of methods, and men of arts. He produced the *Great Treasure* and the *Secret Books* kept in a pillow within the garden.

The Eight Dukes arrived at the gate.

Ge Hong's *Biographies of Divine Immortals* records that Liu An, the King of Huainan, was the grandson of Emperor Gao of the Han. He was humble toward scholars and sincerely loved Confucian learning. Practitioners of methods traveled from a thousand miles away, drawn by his humble words and heavy gifts, to request an audience.

# Dreams.

->By M.W. FRATER DR. W. WYNN WESTCOTT, IX°.<-
->Supreme Magus, Soc. Ros. in Ang.<-

DREAMS have at all times been a favourite subject for discussion, and the very little that is known about their causation has led to the utmost divergence in the opinions expressed concerning them.
All of us dream occasionally, and many persons dream as often as they sleep; probably we all do so, and the difference between persons as to dreaming is due to a variation in the power of Remembrance when awaking.
There is considerable evidence to show that animals dream as well as men, women, and children. Many of us must have observed the domestic cat and dog showing signs of dreaming by their movements and the sounds they make. Tennyson wrote—
> “ Like a dog he hunts in dreams—— ”
It has been said that animals in their wild state of nature do not dream, but it is difficult to make observations on wild animals. It is generally agreed that domestication is the cause of increased mind-power in some animals, and with enlarged powers of observation and concerted action, may come the faculty of dreaming. Domesticated animals certainly develop some Reason in addition to their primal Instinct, and this can only be due to the companionship of man and the training they receive; the mere change of food would not alone account for their extended powers.
To return to humanity, Byron wrote of dreams—
> “ Strange state of being . . . .
> Senseless to feel, and with sealed eyes to see ” ;
while Cato said—
> “ Regard not dreams, since they are but the images, of our hopes and fears.”
Wordsworth said that we may
> “ Hunt half a day for a forgotten dream.”
Joel, the old Hebrew prophet said—
> “ Your old men shall dream dreams,”
Dryden wrote—
> “ Dreams are interludes which fancy makes,”

# To the Most Serene and
## Most Mighty Sovereign and Lord/ Lord
### Gustav of Sweden/ King of the Goths and
### Wends &c./ my most Gracious
### Lord.

<meta>Large woodcut ornamental initial V featuring intricate floral and scrollwork designs, used to open the main body of the dedication text.</meta>

To describe the entire world as is my intention in this book, Most Mighty and Gracious Lord, requires a far-reaching and well-informed mind that has read much, seen much, heard much, and experienced much. Yet all this would still not be enough if a right judgment were not present, by which one might distinguish the true from the false, and the certain from the uncertain. After the books of Holy Scripture, there would be no reading on earth more pleasant and useful to man than the reading of histories, if they were written (as they should be) without regard for this or that party. For what are all histories other than illustrative examples in which one sees how this or that matter turned out? They show how human wisdom and foresight are so often uncertain, even blind, and how all things depend entirely on the hand of God, who works all things in all things. All our counsel goes backward where it is not in accordance with the providence of God. Look: the children of Adam wanted to build a tower reaching to heaven to escape the future flood. How far they failed is manifest to everyone. Ninus and Semiramis undertook to build invincible cities, namely Nineveh and Babylon. They made walls around them so wide that several wagons might go side by side. But it helped them nothing, as was found with time. The Romans wanted to claim for themselves an eternal reign and highest empire over the whole world. For that reason they also destroyed the African city of Carthage, which also undertook such a thing. But how long did they keep it? The Jews and after them the heathens wanted to root out Christ and his wholesome teaching against the counsel of God, but what did they accomplish? The Jews went to ruin because of it, and the heathens were taken from their error and false religion, however much they initially raged against it. The Holy Land formerly flowed with milk and honey, but now it is a smoky, bitter, and wild soil. Greece in those same times had the most ingenious and subtle men that could be found in the world, where also all philosophers and masters of nature arose. What does it have now but wretched, coarse, unlearned, and simple people? Sweden, Gothland, Norway and other northern lands were formerly so poor and needy in bodily sustenance that they could not raise their <term>indigenas</term> <gloss>natives</gloss> and countrymen. Instead, they sent them in large crowds into fertile lands. From there came the Goths, Lombards, Northmen, Cimbri, Swiss, Alemanni and many others. But in our times they surpass almost all lands of Europe in riches. Is there less found in them than in these outer lands? Where does one find more gold, silver, copper, and also other metals than in these lands? Where does one find handsomer cattle, and more meat and fish than in these lands? They give enough dried and salted fish to all of Germany, France, Bohemia and Poland. Everyone knows what precious skins and furs or lining-work come out of these lands into all southern countries. But where does it come from, that these lands which formerly could not nourish their inhabitants now feed them and send nourishment into other lands? It comes from the hand of God, who gives and

# To His Royal Majesty of Sweden.

and takes away according to his pleasure. He shows with his deeds that he is the Lord, not only in heaven but also on earth and in the wide sea. All things are handled through him, and nothing <term>ex fortuna uel casu</term> <gloss>from fortune or chance</gloss>, as men speak of it, but everything happens out of the knowledge, indeed the order of God. From this it comes that one kingdom ends and another begins; one land becomes rich and another perishes; one city increases and another decreases; one lordship dies out and another rises. In summary, under the moving heavens nothing remains permanent; everything is subject to wonder. From this we should learn to set our hearts not on the perishable, but on the eternal. I write such things, however, not to teach Your Royal Majesty, who knows this well, but to give some indication of what caused me to describe this book. The argument extends very far. I wanted to dedicate here a compendium and short summary of all the lands of the earth to the common man, to delight himself therein with reading. I also wanted to show a way to the learned how one might yet write very useful Cosmographies and Topographies after so many German Chronographies. I undertook and began this work eighteen years ago, following that highly learned man Strabo. But while I was still occupied with this work six years ago, Your Royal Majesty's servant came to me, the highly learned Master Georgius Normannus. He was already familiar with me from several books published under my name. When he inspected this undertaken work, it seemed to him well worthy that it should come to light under the royal protection of Your Royal Majesty. Otherwise, I would not have been so bold as to present such a patron for this book. I also undertook this suggestion all the more gladly as I heard from him of the free and inclined spirit which Your Royal Majesty bears toward all the learned and skillful. This has been especially proven in that Your Majesty has been diligent to instruct the young princes, Your Royal Majesty's sons, in Christian virtues and noble arts. May God confirm such a spirit until the end. I would have gladly included Your Royal Majesty's capital city Stockholm, along with other noble cities of the kingdom of Sweden, in this third edition as I have with other cities. By this I would have shown a thankful spirit for the kindness shown to me by Your Royal Majesty. But after Your Royal Majesty most graciously wrote to me from the Royal Castle of Kalmar in the year of Christ 1546, no certain messenger has reached me from such a distance until this today. Thereby I might have revealed my intention to Your Royal Majesty. And with this I wish to have excused myself. I will also henceforth commend myself to Your Royal Majesty most submissively and with the highest diligence. Dated at Basel on the 17th day of March, in the year after Christ's birth 1550.

# Vorred Sebastiani Munsteri
## in das Buch der Cosmography
### oder Weltbeschreibung.

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Ornamental decorative initial 'D' featuring interlaced foliate and vine patterns.</image-desc>Die kunst / so man mit einem Griechischen wort Cosmographiam nennt / das ist beschreibung der Welt / oder Geographiam / beschreibung des Erdreichs / wie hoch und Edel sie allwegen geachtet sey / bey den erfahrnen Männern / zeigen uns alle Historien an / ja die Historie gründe sich auch auff diese kunst / und ohn sie mag niemand ein Histori ordenlichen beschreiben / oder auch recht verstohn / wie dann ein weyser und gelehrter Mann spricht / <margin>Was Geography ist.</margin> Die Geography ist ein erkantnuß des Erdreichs / das wir tödlichen auß der gaben Gottes einwohnen / welche die Kunst liebhaber richtig unnd fertig macht zu verston die geschehenen ding / so uns von alter zeit her in Geschrifften verlassen seind. Ja diese Kunst eröffnet uns zum dickern mal die verborgne heimlichkeit der Heyligen geschrifft / und entblößt die krafft der klügen natur / so do verborgen ligt in mancherley dingen. Wie hetten die Alten / ja auch die so zu unserer zeit leben / also glückhafftig Krieg mögen füren in frembden und ferren Ländern / do sie etwann über hohe Berg / etwann über tieffe Wasser haben müssen reysen / auch etwann über Möre Schiffen / wann sie nicht hetten gewüst durch die Kunst gelegenheit des Erdreichs / weyte und ende des Möres / unnd eigenschafft der Länder : Was meinst du das die König in Hispania für kosten und schaden haben erlitten / biß sie das undertheil des Erdreichs haben erfaren / und die Schiffung von Hispania in Orient durch den Mittag erkündiget ? Man achtet vor zeiten die Menschen hochverständig unnd klüg / die do weit gewandlet unnd an vil enden gewesen waren / vil Stätt gesehen / der Menschen sitten und eygenschafft / gewonheit und gebreuchen erfaren / darzu mancherley Thier / Bäum <margin>In was achtung bey den alten die Cosmography.</margin> und der Kreüter natur hetten gelehrt und erkennt. Man entboth jnen grosse ehre / unnd braucht sie zu Rhäten gemeines nutzes / unnd zu Richtern des Volcks / als die jhenen so durch eygen erfarung güte unnd sälige Rhät geben köndten. Dann diese Kunst streckt sich nit allein uber die Länder / wohnungen und sitten mancherley Völcker / sonder bekümmert sich auch mit andern dingen des Erdreichs und Möres / als mit seltzamen Thieren / Bäumen / Metallen und andern nützen unnd unnützen dingen / so auff dem Erdreich oder in dem Möre erfunden werden. Zu unsern zeiten ist es gar von nöten / das du weyt hin und her auff der Erden umbschweyfest / zu besichtigen unnd erfaren gelegenheit der Länder / Stätt / Wässer / Bergen unnd Thäler. Item die sitten / gebreüch / gesätz / und Regiment der Menschen / eigenschafft unnd natur der Thier / Bäum unnd Kreüter. Du magst diese ding jetzund in den Büchern finden / und darauß mehr lernen und erkennen von diesem oder jhenem Land / dann ein andrer / der gleich darinn jhar unnd tag ist gewesen. Hie findest du wie man zu unsern zeiten also scheinbarlich und Burgerlich under einandern in den gemeinden lebt / weder zu den alten und ersten zeiten / da die Menschen auff der Erden schlecht / einfeltig / ja frech unnd roh lebten. Sie hetten kein verzeichnete Müntz im brauch / do was kein gewerb noch Kaufft handel / sunder sie gaben waht umb waht / und vergolten ein gutthat mit der andern. Es hett keiner etwas besonders oder eygenthumb / sonder wie der Lufft unnd Himmel gemein ware / also was auch das Erdreich unnd Wasser frey bey jederman.

->Sie<-

# Preface of Sebastian Münster
## to the Book of Cosmography
### or Description of the World.

<meta>Ornamental decorative initial D featuring interlaced foliate and vine patterns.</meta> All histories show us how highly and nobly the art called by a Greek word <term>Cosmographiam</term> <gloss>Cosmography</gloss>, that is, description of the world, or <term>Geographiam</term> <gloss>Geography</gloss>, description of the earth, has always been regarded by experienced men. Indeed, history is based on this art, and without it no one can describe a history in an orderly way or rightly understand it. As a wise and learned man says, <margin>What Geography is.</margin> Geography is a knowledge of the earth, which we mortals inhabit by the gift of God, which makes the lovers of art ready and prepared to understand the things that have happened, which have been left to us in writings from ancient times. Indeed, this art frequently opens to us the hidden secrets of Holy Scripture and reveals the power of clever nature that lies hidden in various things. How could the ancients, and also those who live in our time, have conducted wars so successfully in foreign and distant lands? They sometimes had to travel over high mountains, sometimes over deep waters, and also sail over seas. This would have been impossible if they had not known through the art the location of the earth, the width and end of the sea, and the properties of the lands. What do you think the kings in Spain suffered in costs and damages until they explored the lower part of the earth and discovered the navigation from Spain to the Orient through the south? In former times, people were considered highly intelligent and wise who had traveled far and been to many places, seen many cities, and experienced the manners and properties, customs and usages of people. They also learned and recognized many animals, trees <margin>In what regard Cosmography was held by the ancients.</margin> and the nature of herbs. Great honor was offered to them, and they were used as counselors for the common good and as judges of the people, as those who could give good and blessed advice through their own experience. For this art extends not only over the lands, dwellings and customs of various peoples, but also concerns itself with other things of the earth and sea, such as strange animals, trees, metals and other useful and useless things that are found on the earth or in the sea. In our times it is quite necessary that you wander far and wide on the earth to inspect and experience the location of lands, cities, waters, mountains and valleys. Likewise the manners, customs, laws, and government of people, and the properties and nature of animals, trees and herbs. You may now find these things in books and learn and recognize more from them about this or that land than another who has been there for a year and a day. Here you find how people in our times live so visibly and civilly among each other in communities, compared to the old and first times when people on earth lived poorly, simply, even boldly and crudely. They had no marked coins in use; there was no trade or merchant business, but they gave item for item and repaid one good deed with another. No one had anything special or private property, but just as the air and heaven were common, so also the earth and water were free to everyone.

->They<-

<summary>Münster defines geography and cosmography as essential tools for understanding history, scripture, and warfare. He contrasts the modern civil world with the simple, communal life of ancient times.</summary>

Thus, having seen the variety of the <term>passaggi</term> <gloss>vocal runs/ornaments</gloss> made by me for the parts that sing alone, I will not be necessitated to make other demonstration of it, as I had thought. One may, in the part of the Bass (which at times seeks the strings of the Tenor), and in the two following Tenors, observe the rules used by me regarding the syllables, both long and short. First, to perform the preliminary retreat <term>nyenpa</term>: go to a secluded and pleasant place such as a charnel ground, and perform sweeping and so on to make the mind engaged. In that place, in front of yourself, make a mandala of one cubit. In its center, make a circle of one span. In its center, draw a single surplus-offering for the precious support. On top and outside of that, arrange heaps of grain. On the central heap, place a small table or a supreme footed-throne. On top of that, place a skull-cup <term>kapala</term> with the required marks, filled with the "glory-food" <term>palshö</term> and various kinds of blood, and arrange a single support <term>gtor ma</term>.

<leaf-break/>

...Offer many things that have been made, and make requests for the desired goals. Then, perform the preliminary retreat. As before, perform the generation and visualization at the four times of the day, and offer the <term>gtor ma</term>. Thus, practice for twenty-one days and keep it secret. Then, offer the support <term>gtor ma</term> in a clean place. Making the jewel and the body-form is the preliminary retreat. 
Then, for the accomplishment of the actual siddhi <term>spiritual attainment</term>: for the practice of this, on top of the previous altar, make a triangle one span in width and height. Coat its exterior and interior in red with blood and so on. In its three corners, plant three supreme ritual daggers <term>phur ba</term>. On top of it, place a skull-cup with the required marks, filled with various kinds of food. Also, pour various grains, grapes, and fruits inside it. Place various jewels there too. Inside it, place various kinds of food that you enjoy. On top of that, place the aforementioned jewel and the body-form. In the three corners and the front of the mandala, provide four <term>gtor ma</term> made of dough and beer, with small finger-pressed offerings...
